response.title: How long will a power station run a Starlink Mini and two laptops for a workday in a camper, and do I need a solar panel?
response.answer:
For a camper workday running a Starlink Mini and two laptops, I'd recommend a 1,000–1,500Wh portable power station. That should cover a typical 8-hour workday, although laptop power consumption makes a big difference.

A solar panel is optional for a single day, but becomes much more useful if you're working off-grid for several days.

1. How much power will you use?

Here is a realistic estimate for an 8-hour workday, assuming both laptops are being used for normal office work, video calls, and browsing.

These are estimates of actual average consumption, not the maximum wattages printed on laptop chargers.

After accounting for power conversion losses and battery reserve, a practical planning target is 900–1,500Wh of battery capacity.

Assuming an average combined load of 120W and approximately 85% usable energy:

If your laptops have good internal batteries and only need occasional charging, a 1,024Wh station could be sufficient.

3. Do you need solar?

For a single workday, no, provided you start with a sufficiently charged power station.

5. One important efficiency tip

Using DC or USB-C outputs where compatible can reduce losses from converting battery DC power to AC and back again. Make sure the power station has enough independently rated USB-C ports for both laptops and Starlink.

My suggested setup: a 1,500Wh LiFePO₄ power station, plus a 200–400W portable solar panel if you regularly camp without electrical hookups.

One question that would help narrow this down: Are your two laptops MacBooks, typical Windows laptops, or high-powered gaming/workstation laptops? That could change the required battery size substantially.
markup:
For a camper workday running a **Starlink Mini and two laptops**, I'd recommend a **1,000–1,500Wh portable power station**. That should cover a typical 8-hour workday, although laptop power consumption makes a big difference.

A solar panel is optional for a single day, but becomes much more useful if you're working off-grid for several days.

## 1. How much power will you use?

Here is a realistic estimate for an 8-hour workday, assuming both laptops are being used for normal office work, video calls, and browsing.

| Device | Average power | Energy over 8 hours |
|---|---:|---:|
| Starlink Mini | 25–40W | 200–320Wh |
| Laptop 1 | 30–60W | 240–480Wh |
| Laptop 2 | 30–60W | 240–480Wh |
| **Total** | **85–160W** | **680–1,280Wh** |

These are estimates of actual average consumption, not the maximum wattages printed on laptop chargers.

After accounting for power conversion losses and battery reserve, a practical planning target is **900–1,500Wh of battery capacity**.

## 2. How long will different battery sizes last?

Assuming an average combined load of 120W and approximately 85% usable energy:

| Power station capacity | Estimated runtime | 8-hour workday? |
|---|---|---|
| 500Wh | 3.5 hours | No |
| 768Wh | 5.4 hours | Unlikely |
| 1,024Wh | 7.3 hours | Borderline |
| 1,500Wh | 10.6 hours | Yes |
| 2,048Wh | 14.5 hours | Yes, with reserve |

If your laptops have good internal batteries and only need occasional charging, a 1,024Wh station could be sufficient.

## 3. Do you need solar?

For a single workday, **no**, provided you start with a sufficiently charged power station.

For consecutive days off-grid, I'd consider a 200–400W solar setup.

</box>

A 200W panel can meaningfully extend your runtime, but may not fully replenish your daily usage. A 400W panel has a better chance of sustaining a typical workday, assuming good sunlight.

## 4. Calculate your own setup

{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState(1024)}
{@body const [starlink,setStarlink] = DIL.useState(30)}
{@body const [laptop,setLaptop] = DIL.useState(45)}
{@body const [hours,setHours] = DIL.useState(8)}
{@body const [solar,setSolar] = DIL.useState("0")}
{@body const draw = starlink+2*laptop}
{@body const need = draw*hours}
{@body const battery = capacity*0.85}
{@body const solarEnergy = Number(solar)*4*0.75}
{@body const runtime = battery/draw}
<box border radius="2xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Battery capacity**
    <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{capacity.toLocaleString()} Wh</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={256} max={3072} step={128} value={capacity} onChange={setCapacity}/>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Starlink Mini draw**
    <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{starlink} W</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={20} max={40} step={5} value={starlink} onChange={setStarlink}/>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Average draw per laptop**
    <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{laptop} W</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={15} max={90} step={5} value={laptop} onChange={setLaptop}/>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Workday duration**
    <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{hours} hours</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={4} max={12} step={1} value={hours} onChange={setHours}/>
  <text weight="medium" size="sm">Solar panel size</text>
  <radio-group direction="col" value={solar} onChange={setSolar}>
    <radio value="0">No solar</radio>
    <radio value="200">200W</radio>
    <radio value="400">400W</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <grid columns={2} gap={3}>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} gap={1}>
        <caption>Battery-only runtime</caption>
        <title size="xl" color="default" tabularNums>{runtime.toFixed(1)} hrs</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} gap={1}>
        <caption>Daily energy demand</caption>
        <title size="xl" color="default" tabularNums>{need.toLocaleString()} Wh</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <box gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      <text weight="medium" size="sm">Workday energy coverage</text>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs" tabularNums>{Math.round(Math.min(100,(battery+solarEnergy)/need*100))}%</text>
    </row>
    <box background="surface-tertiary" height="12px" radius="full" clip>
      <box background={battery+solarEnergy>=need?"success-solid":"warning-solid"} height="100%" width={`${Math.min(100,(battery+solarEnergy)/need*100)}%`} radius="full"/>
    </box>
    <row align="center" gap={2}>
      {#if battery+solarEnergy>=need}
        <icon name="check-circle" color="success"/>
        <text color="success" size="sm">Estimated energy is sufficient for your workday.</text>
      {:else}
        <icon name="alert-circle" color="caution"/>
        <text size="sm">Estimated shortfall: {Math.ceil(need-battery-solarEnergy)}Wh.</text>
      {/if}
    </row>
    <caption>Solar estimate assumes 4 peak-sun-hours and 75% solar-system efficiency. Energy coverage is not a guarantee of continuous power, since solar production varies during the day.</caption>
  </box>
</box>

## 5. One important efficiency tip

Starlink officially specifies 20–40W average consumption and supports DC power, including a 100W USB-C PD source with its compatible cable. <Cite refs={["turn576709search0","turn576709search1"]}/>

Using DC or USB-C outputs where compatible can reduce losses from converting battery DC power to AC and back again. Make sure the power station has enough independently rated USB-C ports for both laptops and Starlink.

**My suggested setup:** a 1,500Wh LiFePO₄ power station, plus a 200–400W portable solar panel if you regularly camp without electrical hookups.

One question that would help narrow this down: **Are your two laptops MacBooks, typical Windows laptops, or high-powered gaming/workstation laptops?** That could change the required battery size substantially.

| 1,500Wh | 10.6 hours | Yes |
| 2,048Wh | 14.5 hours | Yes, with reserve |

If your laptops have good internal batteries and only need occasional charging, a 1,024Wh station could be sufficient.

## 3. Do you need solar?

For a single workday, **no**, provided you start with a sufficiently charged power station.

For consecutive days off-grid, I'd consider a 200–400W solar setup.
